messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan is a 36-year-old tax consultant who came to treatment at his wife’s urging after months of growing tension at home and increasing strain at work. Before entering civilian life he had served in the military, and the event he returns to came during a patrol when a routine conversation broke apart into shouting, confusion, and sudden violence. What stays with him is not a clean sequence so much as sharply preserved fragments: the metallic taste that flooded his mouth as he hit the ground, the strange deadness that cut through him for moments even while things were happening, and the way the emotional force of it still becomes unbearable when the memory breaks through. He says there are times he can tell the story in a flat, detached way, almost as if it happened to someone else, and other times he starts to remember and has to stop because he is suddenly overwhelmed.

In the years since leaving the military, the memory has attached itself to ordinary situations in a way Ethan finds humiliating and hard to explain. At the office, when client meetings turn confrontational or a discussion shifts toward certain charged topics, he can feel the event rushing back before he has fully registered why. On bad days this also happens when he feels physically unwell—lightheaded, nauseated, or run down—because the bodily state itself seems to match something from then. In those moments he is not just reminded in a general way; he can taste again what he tasted during the event, and the force of that sensory return is enough to shut him down. Because he has learned that these moments can pull the memory into the room with him, he avoids talking about what happened, changes the subject when conversations edge too close, and pulls away from emotional closeness when his wife tries to comfort him.

At home, his wife has been especially distressed by how sharply he reacts to touch. If she puts a hand on his shoulder from behind while he is washing dishes or sitting quietly, he startles violently before he has time to recognize her. Ethan has come to live with a constant sense that danger announces itself in subtle ways, especially in silence. A room going unusually quiet makes him scan immediately, as if something is about to happen, and wherever he goes—restaurants, conference rooms, even his own church—he identifies exits before he can settle. These habits are not abstract precautions to him. The memory carries such intense bodily force that he feels he has to be ready for it, and for whatever might come with it, at any moment. The more the memory intrudes, the more convinced he becomes that vigilance is necessary.

That vigilance, however, seems to make the world narrower and more charged. Because Ethan is always tracking silence, shifts in tone, and who is standing where, confrontations feel charged almost before they begin, and certain topics seem dangerous the instant they arise. At work he now chooses seats near the door in client meetings and spends part of the meeting monitoring how he would leave if he needed to. If a discussion becomes tense, the alertness in his body intensifies so quickly that the old fragments begin to press in again. He has noticed, too, that after a spell of scanning and bracing himself, even feeling physically off for ordinary reasons can become a trigger; once he detects weakness or nausea, his mind leaps toward the event.

Over time Ethan has organized his life around not setting any of this off. He avoids being touched, keeps conversation away from the military and its aftermath, and tries not to let himself feel too happy or relaxed because positive feelings seem unsafe, as though letting down his guard would leave him exposed. That emotional pushing-away has had costs. His wife experiences him as absent even when he is physically present, and he knows there are evenings when he seems cold or unreachable. Yet the strategy makes sense to him because strong feeling of any kind can open the door to the memory, and once it begins he fears being swept into something he cannot control. Even the numb, emotionless version of recall is not reassuring; it leaves him shaken in a different way, uneasy that his mind can go so blank around something so important.

What finally brought him in was a recent incident at work during tax season. A client became argumentative during a meeting about a disputed filing, the room fell quiet in the aftermath, and Ethan found himself already mapping the exits, tasting that old metallic flavor, and unable to stay present. When a colleague touched his arm afterward, he jerked back so hard that everyone noticed. He went home ashamed and exhausted, and when his wife later tried to ask what had happened, he shut the conversation down almost immediately. Sitting in treatment now, Ethan is frightened that his life is being organized more and more by avoiding reminders and staying on guard. What he hopes, though cautiously, is not to erase what happened but to stop feeling as if any silence, any confrontation, or any unexpected touch can pull him right back into it.
